specifi c components for use with DIY favorites including Wordpress, ExpressionEngine,
Drupal, Joomla, and other social software platforms. For nearly any online social plat-
form, there is an associated curation solution: If the platform you are using does not
support curation (again, most do), consider strongly moving to one that does.
Why This Matters in Business
Absent the ability to curate, the progression to higher forms of engagement is effec-
tively stopped. In nearly any act of sharing, for example, there is at least an implied
sense of rating: “If (I) didn’t think some particular piece of content was worth (your)
--- page 355 ---
time then (I) would not have shared it with you.” Beyond the polar “share/don’t share”
as a surrogate for curation, more finely grained ratings and reviews, testimonials and
other forms of direct, overt curation provide participants in social business applica-
tions with a direct pathway to collaboration. Providing the ability for customers and
stakeholders to publicly comment and share opinions is essential in drawing people
into your social applications and thereby moving participants ultimately toward collab-
orative involvement in your business or organization.
Crowdsourcing
Crowdsourcing—turning to the Social Web and its participants en masse for input to
specific challenges or needs—is a social activity that directly drives collaboration: Like
ideation, covered separately in the next section, crowdsourcing not only makes “every-
one a participant” but does so in a way that provides public credit for this participa-
tion. In doing so, crowdsourcing encourages future participation and build “stickiness”
with regard to that social application.
333
That crowdsourcing applications have the ability to grow and develop an audi-   ■
ence over time is a significant plus: Crowdsourcing applications can be used as a part   Soci
of a larger social business program to not only pull participants in, but also to keep   a
l
them involved over the longer term. This is especially helpful when your objectives   A
include both the need to solve a problem or challenge that is suitable for crowdsourcing   pplicat
and also to simultaneously build and sustain a community or similar social structure in
the context of your business.   ions
In business applications, crowdsourcing often takes the basic form of pub-   Dr
licly asking for ideas or suggestions against a specific business objective. Building   i v e
on consumption and curation, crowdsourcing is a viable method for accomplishing
specific types of tasks that appropriately involve your customers or stakeholders. The   Engagem
development of confidential or proprietary processes, for example, is clearly an inter-
en
nal matter, so in these cases consider an internal crowdsourcing application: Dell’s   t
“EmployeeStorm,” or Ford’s use of the Covisint ideation and collaboration platform
across its suppliers network are solid examples.
What is suitable for crowdsourcing? Designing a logo, supporting a cause,
providing answers to a question, and similar challenges where a diversity of ideas or
talents contributing to the solution are all possibilities. Building on a wiki—a col-
laborative document framework that is itself an example of crowdsourcing—Anjali
Ramachandran has compiled a list (see sidebar) of business-related crowdsourcing
examples. Robert Scoble offers a similar list: Search the Web for “crowdsourcing
examples”—and you’ll find plenty more, ranging from design challenges to lawn
­mowing services to the top apps for mobile phones.

Pepsi’s “Refresh” project, referenced in detail in Chapter 7, “Five Essential Tips,”
along with Coke’s “Fannovation,” referenced in Chapter 4, are likewise examples of
crowdsourcing. In both cases, the brands involved are appealing directly to those par-
ticipating in these social applications to direct the efforts of the brands according to the
business objectives as they relate the respective programs. In the case of Fannovation,
--- page 357 ---
the objective is the association of Coke with NCAA sports, accomplished by linking
the brand with the crowdsourcing application built around the NCAA fan experience.
In the case of Refresh, the business objective is linking the brand—Pepsi—with the
causes of its participants through a corporate social responsibility program directed not
through an internal committee but directly and transparently through a crowdsourcing
application.
Why This Matters in Business
Directly involving customers, stakeholders, potential customers, and others in appro-
priate collaborative activities conveys to these participants a sense of ownership and
control—a stake in the brand, so to speak—that is not possible in a read-only context.
Not only does crowdsourcing offer the potential of better outcomes— as defined by
those who participate in such programs—but also further moves these same partici-
pants “up” the engagement ladder, ultimately toward brand advocacy.

Ideation platforms are a powerful class of social applications that lend them-
selves to both business management (for example, process, product, or service inno-   ions

specific practice of pulling customers into the business-design process—is important   i v e

Second, by opening up at least part of the responsibility for collective thinking
outside of the current thought leaders, the entire pool of ideas is expanded, driving
not only product and service-level change but also process change. Along with better
“things” come better ways to make those things. These are exactly the results noted
by Starbucks, Dell, Germany’s Tchibo, and Intuit’s Small Business community, all of
whom are using the ideation platforms as ways to improve their respective businesses
by forging collaborative relationships with their customers.
What really makes an ideation platform work is not the “idea solicitation” per
se. After all, how many people really believe that anything actually happens as a result
of an anonymous note dropped in a suggestion box? The problem with the classic sug-
gestion box—anonymous or not—is that the suggestion acceptance process and any
--- page 358 ---
actual outcomes are not visible to the person making the suggestion. In other words,
there is a lack of transparency, a lack of accountability (on both sides), and therefore a
lack of significance. “Why bother?” is the most common response, and the opportunity
to gather real feedback is lost.
Note that this loss of feedback happens inside and outside the business. In India,
more so than any other place I’ve been, following nearly any service delivery in a restau-
rant, pub, airline flight, etc., I am offered a comment and feedback card. What happens
with the data collected is not always clear, though this much I do know: I have received
personal responses from Kingfisher Airlines following comments and suggestions that I
have made using the in-flight comment cards—shown in Figure 12.6—that are always
offered onboard Kingfisher flights. The result is that, at least when flying on Kingfisher,
I always fill out the comment card and add a personal note if I have something addi-
tional to offer.

The Kingfisher example provides a key insight into the requirements for socially
linking a business, its customers, and its employees: visibility and accountability. The
ideation platforms, more than anything else, bring total transparency to the suggestion
and feedback processes. Ideas are publicly submitted where they are visible to everyone
(content creation and consumption). Next, they are voted up or down by participants
at large (curation). Finally, the business stakeholders—a Product Manager, for exam-
ple—selects from the highest ranked items and offers various versions for implementa-
tion, which are then reviewed again by the participant community (collaboration). The
resulting innovations become additional bonding points for customers as credit is given
back to them. The entire process is visible, and the outcome—the actual disposition of
any given suggestion—is clear to everyone.
--- page 359 ---
Note that ideation comes in many forms: In addition to purpose-built ideation
platforms, small groups of personally invited participants can be very effective: As
an example, consider the specifi cally invited LEGO fans who helped design LEGO
Mindstorms, or impromptu feedback sessions with larger groups as a part of existing
industry events. Ideation, while it is the formal name given to this new-style transpar-
ent suggestion process, does not itself have to be formal.

is a powerful loop. Check out the My Starbucks Idea site, or even better visit a store

Support Communities
If ideation is the “fresh thinking” business application built around the practice of
crowdsourcing that delivers ideas into business and organizations, then support com-
munities—again, these are social applications—are the analogous tools that deliver
needed information and solutions back to customers, based on the combined principles
of crowdsourcing and direct customer empowerment.
When Dell set out to rebuild its customer service program, Dell’s internal teams
noticed something: In its existing online (and offl ine) support environment, there
existed customers who really wanted to see Dell succeed, customers who often had
some of the answers that were needed in the course of fi elding support issues. Inside
Dell, something clicked: If there were customers who had specifi c knowledge that could
benefi t other customers, and if these same customers were also Dell advocates, could
they be directly tapped to help Dell improve and scale its customer service program?
This is the thinking that in part gave rise to the now rebuilt Dell support
338   communities, and it uncovered a basic fact that is common across many industries:
■   Customers are often experts—at least as regards their use of a product or service—and
IONS   as such are in collective possession of a sizeable body of knowledge. Properly applied,
this collective body of knowledge can radically change their experience as customers.
PPLICAT
The problem is that this knowledge is largely unstructured, and it’s distributed in ways
A L   that make actual bits of knowledge hard to spot when they are really needed.

12:   correct answers—in public, to other customers—support forums make it easy for cus-
r e   tomers to tap the larger collective, to self-serve and quickly solve their own problems.

answers as they are so moved. Over time, that extensive body of knowledge contained
in the minds of customers is reexpressed in the support forum discussions where it is
curated (“this solution works/this solution doesn’t”), organized, and tagged so that it
can be found and applied by those in need.

Why This Matters in Business
Participant-driven support forums provide the possibility of both improved service
and the actual determination of ROI. Service may be improved, for example, because
the support forum is available 24x7, including all day on gift-giving holidays when the
need for support typically spikes, and because the larger body of participants will often
have more answers for more issues. Because customers themselves often possess a deep
body of collective knowledge about how to fix, extend—think LEGO Mindstorms
here, where enthusiasts hack the internal control programs and publish their findings
for use by the Mindstorm community—and in general get more out the products and
services they purchase, support forums become central to the redefined, collaborative
customer experience.
Finally, an answer too on the ROI question: Support calls have a known cost.
Support incidents that are fully resolved in a support forum represent a call-center cost
avoided, leading directly to formal ROI measures and standards to which even the
CFO will give two thumbs up.   339

nizational preparations that precede the implementation of a social business effort.

Internal Readiness: Workflow and Your Response Plan
Coincident with your external social technology plan, begin early the process of iden-
tifying and recruiting colleagues across business units for the development of your
cross-functional social technology team. Need help getting started? Go back to the
identified business objectives: Who has profit responsibility associated with those
objectives? Those are good people to start with. Add representatives from your legal
team: They can help you create effective social media policies that are consistent with
the culture of your firm or organization. HR and Finance/Compliance are part of this
too: Sarbanes-Oxley, in the United States, and the unfettered employee use of social
--- page 367 ---
technology—including by employees when outside the workplace—can be a trouble-
some mix, to say the least. Customer Support is as well a great potential partner in
your social technology planning process.
Workflow is an important factor in your implementation, so look for intel-
ligence tools (for example, social media listening and analytics platforms) that offer
robust workflow support. Refer back to the flowchart (see Chapter 1, “Social Media
and Customer Engagement”) developed by the U.S. Air Force for systematizing your
response efforts. In particular, consider who will actually respond, and create estimates
for the amount of time a response to a tweet or blog post will require and then build
this into your cost and effort plan for the upcoming period. Attention to details like
this will pay huge dividends as you ramp up collaborative social media programs.

Review of the Main Points
Review the main points covered in Chapter 12, listed below. Consider these as you
begin to develop your overall plan for the integration of social technology in your busi-
ness or organization.
•   S ocial applications tie social objects and social graphs together. Simply put,
people connect with other people around the things that interest them in order
to accomplish tasks that improve their lives.
•   I nternal readiness—the capability to respond and to address business challenges
holistically rather than functionally—is an element of your social technology
implementation effort.
--- page 369 ---
•   S ocial technology begins with business objectives. Don’t let the technology
guide your implementation, but instead let your objectives guide the technology
selection.
In summary, unless you are ready to tackle Enterprise 2.0 (or you are working in
an organization that is already doing this), the starting point in applying social technol-
ogy to business is in connecting your customers and stakeholders through collabora-
tive processes that link business objectives with the higher levels of engagement. You
can speed this process within your own functional area with the assistance of informal
cross-functional teams. Take the time to build support in other parts of your business,
and you’ll find the entire process significantly easier. The typical starting point—after
the implementation of a listening program—is generally connecting your business pres-
ence into the existing social spaces where customers spend time, setting up an effective
listen-understand-respond process. That is then followed by the implementation—as
driven by your business objectives—of collaborative tools such as support and ideation
platforms to drive a basic business norm of “Listen, Understand, Evolve.”   347

Terms and Definitions
In any sufficiently precise study—and the appli-
cation of social technology is certainly no excep-
tion—the need will arise for specific terms that
enable concepts to be translated into actions.
The definitions of many of the terms that are
core to social technology are still evolving; how-
ever, within this book the following have been   351
■
adopted and used consistently. More important   T
er
than agreeing on specific terms—at a general   ms
a n

and then applying these meanings as you develop   ions
your social technology and business programs.

A

other.
Chapter Contents
Social Object

--- page 374 ---
Social Object
Definition: A Social Object is some “thing” we share with others as part
of our social media experience on the Social Web.
Glenn Assheton-Smith, 2009
What It Means and Why It Matters
A social object is something that is inherently talkworthy, something around which
people will naturally congregate and converse. Social objects are an essential element in
the implementation of social technology: Social objects are the anchor points for these
efforts and as such are the “magnets” that hold a community together.
While it may seem like so much semantics, when viewed in the context of the
way in which people are connected or to whom they are connected the social object
352   provides the underlying rationale or motive for being connected at all. In short, with-
■   out the social object, there is no “social.”
ions
t i   Social Application
n i
Def
d   Definition: A Social Application is software that coordinates group inter-
n a   action that is important to running your business.
ms
er   John Milan, ReadWriteWeb, October 12, 2006
T
A:
x di   What It Means and Why It Matters
n
e p   The term social application—expressed in this definition in a decidedly business
p a
context—refers to the specific tools or functions available to participants in a social
network—that is, the tools and functions that allow those participants to perform spe-
cific social tasks such as friending, connecting, sharing, and similar. The social appli-
cation includes larger software components as well, up to and including entire social
networks.
In this sense, it’s the social application that “allows social activity to happen” in
a distributed (e.g., virtual or online) context. In real life, the social application is the
living room sofa, where conversation is facilitated, or the postal system, through which
party invitations and RSVPs are exchanged. In online communities, this same type of
social exchange is facilitated through software applications.
--- page 375 ---
Social Graph
Definition: The Social Graph is the representation of our relationships.
In present day context, these graphs define our personal, family, or busi-
ness communities on social networking websites.
Jeremiah Owyang, 2007
What It Means and Why It Matters
The term social graph refers to the relationships between members of a social network
and the details around the ways in which those members are connected. The social
graph of an individual may extend beyond a single network, in which case this indi-
vidual forms a link between adjacent networks.
The social graph is important in business applications. By understanding the
ways in which participants in a social network are connected, it is possible to predict   353
how information will be transmitted through that network, and therefore the social   ■
graph forms the basis for optimizing business participation in social networks.   Soci
a l
Social Network   CR
M
A social network is a social structure made up of individuals (or orga-
nizations) which are tied (connected) by one or more specific types of
interdependency, such as friendship, kinship, common interest, financial
exchange, dislike, sexual relationships, or relationships of beliefs, knowl-
edge, or prestige.
Wikipedia
What It Means and Why It Matters
The term social network refers to the collective facility—to Facebook or Orkut or the
Intel Developer’s Network and everyone contained within it.
In this sense, the term social network is a noun: it refers to a place (however vir-
tual it may be) where social interactions—aka “social networking”—occurs.
Social CRM
“Social CRM is the company’s response to the customer’s control of the
conversation.”
Paul Greenberg, 2009
--- page 376 ---
What It Means and Why It Matters
Social CRM is a key business concept. It combines the traditional practice of paying
attention to customer data; however, it operates in the social rather than transactional
context. Social CRM connects the conversations that circulate on the Social Web with
the internal decisions and business processes that gave rise to those conversations.
If you are interested (highly recommended), Paul provides a more in-depth ver-
sion of this same definition along with his logic here:
http://the56group.typepad.com/pgreenblog/2009/07/time-to-put-a-stake-in-the-
ground-on-social-crm.html
You can find this quickly by searching for “paul greenberg definition of social
crm” using Google.

Multimedia Tools and Applications (2023) 82:46011–46036
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11042-023-15302-3
A novel technique for classifying Parkinson’s disease using
structural MRI scans
Ketna Khanna1    · Sapna Gambhir1 · Mohit Gambhir2
Received: 22 November 2022 / Revised: 19 January 2023 / Accepted: 6 April 2023 /
Published online: 27 April 2023
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2023
Abstract
Parkinson’s is a movement-related progressive disorder that causes irreversible damage
and heavily derails the patient’s life. PD is generally detected via inspection of symptoms
and family history by neurologists which may be inefficient, time-consuming and costly to
the patient. Although the motor-related signs act as the major contributor to Parkinson’s
detection, these occur in the later stage of the disease when the symptoms have already
intensified. Henceforth, there is a necessity for a Computer Aided Diagnosis (CAD) for an
early yet accurate classification of Parkinson’s. This work proposes a fusion of 3D- Dis-
crete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and a variant of 3D Local Binary Pattern (LBP) on 3D
T1-weighted structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (sMRI) scans acquired from two
publically available databases namely: PPMI and SWADESH for Parkinson’s diagnosis.
The International dataset has been retrieved from the PPMI database and the Indian dataset
has been acquired from SWADESH database. Features have been extracted from the gray
matter. Fisher Discriminant Ratio (FDR) has been utilized for selecting relevant features.
Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression, Random forest and K-NN have been used
for performing classification. The proposed technique achieved a performance accuracy of
92.45% and 90.57% for data acquired from the PPMI database and SWADESH database
respectively. It outperformed the state-of-art techniques with respect to accuracy, sensitiv-
ity and specificity. From the results, it has been concluded that the suggested technique has
the potential for an early yet effective identification of Parkinson’s and can be utilized for
clinical diagnosis by neurologists.
Keywords  Parkinson’s disease · Machine learning · Magnetic resonance imaging · Wavelet
transform · Fisher discriminant ratio · Local binary pattern · SVM · Random forest
* Ketna Khanna
ketnakhanna05@gmail.com
1   J. C. Bose University of Science and Technology, YMCA, Faridabad, Haryana, India 121002
2   Ministry of Education, Delhi, India 110001
Vol.:(0123456789) 1 3

46012   Multimedia Tools and Applications (2023) 82:46011–46036
1  Background
Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a progressive disorder that causes neuro-degeneration within
the brain regions [23]. PD causes structural changes inside the brain and leads to the death
of dopaminergic neurons inside the brain. Dopamine acts as a chemical messenger which
is passed throughout the body via neurons to produce effective communication between
them. Deficiency of dopamine results in communication issues inside the body. Due to
this, the brain starts losing its control thereby resulting in non-movement and movement-
related disabilities [15]. In the initial stage of Parkinson’s, non-movement-related signs like
hallucination, sleep disorder, fluctuations in blood pressure, memory loss, tiredness, pain,
uncontrolled saliva, bladder issues etc. are common [30]. However, PD when progressed,
leads to motor impairments like issues in voluntary movements, shaking, tremors, gait and
balance-related problems, unable to pronounce complex words, masked face and so on.
Even though there is no cure for PD, medicines and exercises may help in controlling
its signs from worsening [7]. The diagnosis of PD comprises manual inspection of its signs
via a neurologist along with questionnaire-based tests like the Mini-Mental State Exami-
nation (MMSE) and Unified Parkinson’s Disease rating Scale (UPDRS) [19]. If a person
has PD but is misdiagnosed, the disease may progress causing permanent damage and it
may become difficult to control it [13]. As of now, more than 10 million people are suf-
fering from Parkinson’s and many may still be undiagnosed (https://​www.​parki​nson.​org/​
Under​stand​ing-​Parki​nsons/​Stati​stics). A person in the later stage of PD becomes helpless
and dependent on others even for daily simple chores like sitting, standing, incontinence,
cognitive functions etc. thereby degrading the quality of life [43].
Recently, Machine Learning (ML) has paved the way in medical diagnosis and image
processing. Researchers have been employing ML techniques for classifying Parkin-
son’s and healthy subjects using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), Positron Emission
Tomography (PET) scans, Single-photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT)
images, voice samples, finger tapping tests, handwritten drawings etc. [2, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12,
14, 18, 24, 34, 36, 40, 48]. Nevertheless, these are unsuitable for clinical applicability
due to relatively poor performances and faulty diagnoses. Therefore, there is a need for a
Computer-aided Diagnosis (CAD) for Parkinson’s early and effective detection that can be
employed clinically.
Parkinson’s results in structural changes within the brain regions. Structural MRI
(sMRI) scans are capable of detecting the anatomical changes within the brain thereby
detecting Parkinson’s. Many studies have utilized sMRI scans for Parkinson’s diagno-
sis. Some have utilized cortical atrophy for its classification [16, 41]. While others have
utilized interior regions of the brain as Region of Interest (ROI) for detecting structural
changes [46, 47]. The regions which may prove as a potential biomarker for PD diagnosis
include the caudate, thalamus, putamen and frontal lobes. However, these studies failed to
recognize that the brain regions are interconnected. Therefore, these may have missed the
crucial regions that may be associated with PD. Henceforth, this study has utilized sMRI
scans. Also, as per the review Gray Matter (GM) has been identified as a potential bio-
marker for PD diagnosis. Henceforth, GM as a whole has been selected as ROI for obtain-
ing the relevant features.
This work has utilized 3D- Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and variations of
3D-LBP for extracting pertinent features. Then the best variation of 3D-LBP i.e. LBP-309
has been combined with 3D-DWT to form the feature vector. To the best of our knowledge,
this combination has not been utilized for Parkinson’s diagnosis. Fisher Discriminant Ratio
1 3
--- page 3 ---
Multimedia Tools and Applications (2023) 82:46011–46036   46013
(FDR) has been used for selecting relevant features. Lastly, the model has been trained
via Support Vector Machine (SVM), random forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR) and
K- Nearest Neighbor (K-NN). Finally, cross-validation has been performed using tenfold
cross-validation.
The organization of this paper is as follows. Section 2 presents the related work. Sec-
tion 3 describes the availability of the dataset. Section 4 presents the pre-processing tech-
niques. Section 5 discusses feature extraction techniques. Section 6 presents feature selec-
tion techniques. Section 7 describes ML techniques and cross-validation. Section 8 presents
the performance analysis. Section 9 presents a discussion and Section 10 concludes.
2  Related work
PD can be detected by analyzing structural changes within the brain regions via Magnetic
Resonance Imaging (MRI). Brain MRI can detect structural changes like brain region
enlargement, brain region shrinkage and Lesions. This section presents a literature review
of Parkinson’s patients vs. healthy controls (HC).
Sabrina Z has suggested a Parkinson’s inspection technique using symptoms, MRI
scans and a hybrid model [37]. The hybrid model is a combination of both MRI scans and
signs of PD. Data has been obtained from the PPMI database. The authors have utilized
an imbalanced dataset. Also, 3D scans have been converted to 2D to reduce their com-
plexity. The MRI-based model has been trained via LR and Convolutional Neural Network
(CNN). The authors believe that manual detection via signs and symptoms is not that reli-
able. However, the MRI-based model achieved a lower accuracy of 77%.
Song C et al. have proposed an sMRI-based Parkinson’s classification technique [45].
According to the authors, the previous studies focused on analyzing modifications in brain
regions at the group level. However, the authors argue that inspection of variations must be
performed at an individual level irrespective of the group. To identify true biomarkers of
Parkinson’s, the authors have extracted features from GM and WM regions. Also, 4 distinct
feature selection techniques namely Relief F, graph theory, recursive feature elimination
(RFE) and stability selection have been utilized to retrieve a minimal set of effective fea-
tures. SVM has been used to train the model. A maximum accuracy of 89.58% has been
achieved by the authors for GM regions.
Chen Y et al. have suggested an sMRI based PD detection technique [11]. UPDRS
scores have also been retrieved by the authors along with T1- weighted sMRI scans for
PD patients and HC. The authors have utilized the thalamus region for extracting relevant
features. As per the experiment, enlarged bilateral thalami and nuclei atrophy have been
observed by the authors. However, the results are inefficient as per the clinical relevance
since the technique has only been applied to an individual region.
Worker A et al. evaluated 18 subcortical ROIs from T1 weighted flair MRI sequences
for identifying Parkinson’s disorder [47]. However, the information regarding the source
of the dataset has been missing from the manuscript. The ROIs have been selected specifi-
cally from the GM regions. The model has been trained via SVM and Leave-one-out cross-
validation (LOOCV). However, the proposed technique has attained an accuracy of 75%.
Soltaninejad S et al. have proposed a novel CAD-based technique for classifying Par-
kinson’s from healthy individuals [44]. T1 weighted MRI scans along with clinical infor-
mation about the subjects have been retrieved from the PPMI database. In the presented
technique, 31 distinct pre-processing techniques have been applied to the MRI scans using
1 3
--- page 4 ---
46014   Multimedia Tools and Applications (2023) 82:46011–46036
FreeSurfer. The pre-processing includes intensity normalization, skull stripping, motion
correction etc. Features have been extracted from seven different regions of the left and
right hemispheres. Lastly, classification has been performed via LR, RF and SVM where
the former outperformed.
Huppertz HJ et al. have proposed a differential diagnostic technique for Parkinson-
ism disorders using MRI modality [16]. The authors believe that changes in atrophy may
classify PD from Parkinsonism. Features have been extracted from the whole brain. SVM
along with stratified tenfold cv has been used for training the suggested model. From the
experiments, the mid-brain, basal ganglia and cerebellar peduncles have been found as the
potential biomarkers for Parkinson’s. The introduced technique achieved a lower accuracy
of 65%.
Liu L et al. have extracted features from GM and WM regions for Parkinson’s detection
[26]. Relevant data has been acquired for axial, sagittal and coronal planes from the PPMI
database. The authors have utilized iterative feature selection based on canonical correla-
tion analysis (CCA) for identifying relevant features. Robust Linear Discriminant Analysis
(RLDA) has been utilized for performing classification.
Chen Y et al. have proposed Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) based technique
for classifying Parkinson’s [10]. The authors believe that this approach can be utilized for
detecting Alzheimer’s and bipolar disorders. The authors have performed classification
concerning 3 labels namely; diseased patients, healthy individuals and noise. SVM has
been used for performing classification.
Salvatore C et al. have introduced a novel technique for the differential diagnosis of
Parkinson’s from Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) [38]. A relatively smaller dataset
has been obtained from an unknown source. Features have been extracted from GM using
PCA, and then Voxel-based Morphometry (VBM) has been utilized for identifying possi-
ble biomarkers. Lastly, classification has been performed using SVM with LOOCV.
Long D et al. have utilized a multi-modality Parkinson’s detection technique using sMRI
and resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) [27]. The authors have applied the proposed
framework to a self-acquired dataset. For sMRI, features have been extracted from WM,
GM and CSF. Whereas features like Regional functional connectivity strength (RFCS),
Amplitude of Low-Frequency Fluctuations (ALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo) have
been retrieved from rsfMRI. For the selection of relevant features, a two-sample t-test has
been utilized. The model has been trained via SVM and LOOCV.
Niels KF et al. have examined the capability of voxel-based morphometry for the dif-
ferential diagnostic technique for classifying PSP, HC and idiopathic Parkinson’s disorder
[31]. The dataset has been retrieved from an unknown source. Features have been extracted
from GM regions using VBM and SVM has been used for performing classification. Anal-
ysis has been performed using the SPM toolbox. However, a relatively lower performance
has been achieved by the suggested model.
A summary of the review for PD vs. HC has been presented in Table 1.

3.1  Databases
The Parkinson’s dataset has been extracted from two sources namely: the Parkinson’s Pro-
gression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database and SWADESH database0. The dataset uti-
lized in this study has been generated using the MPRAGE GRAPPA protocol. Magneti-
zation-Prepared Rapid Gradient-Echo (MPRAGE) is a gradient echo pulse protocol that is
used for the rapid acquisition of T1-weighted sequences [25]. GeneRalized Autocalibrating
Partial Parallel Acquisition (GRAPPA) is a parallel imaging technique that supports high-
resolution acquisitions that too in shorter periods.
3.1.1  PPMI database
Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database was launched by the Michael
J. Fox Foundation in 2010 for its accurate yet early diagnosis and to inspect its progression. It
provides access to the clinical, imaging and biomarker data regarding Parkinson’s (https://​andys​
brain​book.​readt​hedocs.​io/​en/​latest/​fMRI_​Short_​Course/​Prepr​ocess​ing/​Slice_​Timing_​Corre​
ction.​html). “The mission of PPMI is to identify one or more biomarkers of Parkinson’s disease
progression”. It is managed by PPMI Bioinformatics Core, the Laboratory of NeuroImaging
(LONI) at the University of Southern California. It contains Blood samples and MRI data of
international subjects (T1 weighted, T2 weighted, fMRI, SPECT, PET). It comprises raw data as
well as pre-processed neurological images. It comprises around 10,000 neurological images of
diseased people as well as of healthy control consisting of an almost equal number of images
for both genders and having ages ranging from 34–86 years from more than 24 reliable
sources. Blood samples of approx. 500–600 people are also included in the database for research.
3.1.2  Indian dataset
The Indian dataset has been acquired from the SWADESH database (http://​swade​sh.​nbrc.​
res.​in). It is the leading open access multi-modal database for the Indian datasets. It has
been introduced for researchers and clinicians for the purpose of neurological disease
diagnosis and to monitor the progression of the disease. The database includes neuroimag-
ing scans like MRI scans, PET and SPECT images for Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s,
Dementia, Schizophrenia, autism, epilepsy etc. along with the normal subjects.
3.2  Inclusion criteria
The inclusion criteria of the subjects for the study are described below:
3.2.1  Parkinson’s patients
i. Patients over 35 years.
ii. Baseline visit with I or II Hoehn & Yahr (H & Y scale).
iii. Confirmed depletion of dopamine levels in pre-synaptic dopaminergic images.
iv. Irrespective of gender
3.2.2  Healthy subjects
i. Patients over 35 years.

ii. Irrespective of gender.
iii. No ­1st-degree relative of Parkinson’s Patient.
iv. No history of any drug consumption that interferes with dopamine transporter.
v. Absence of any sign of active neurodegenerative disorder.

4  Pre‑processing of dataset
Artefacts and noise can be introduced in the medical images during MRI acquisition [22].
These undesirable substances may deteriorate the MRI scans which may confuse the
pathology. It may also lead to poor diagnostic performance. Thus, the applicability of pre-
processing techniques is vital to prevent misdiagnosis.
In this paper, pre-processing has been performed using Statistical Parametric Mapping
(SPM12) toolbox within Matlab. The following quality enhancement techniques have been
applied to the dataset acquired from the PPMI database [20]:
i. Slice time correction: Slice time correction has been performed on the acquired MRI
scans to correct the slice offset delay. It may magnify the model’s performance.
ii. Realignment: The process of conducting an MRI scan may include certain head
movements by the subject. These movements may impact the processing and assess-
ment of MRI images. Realignment eliminates this head mobility and ensures stillness
in the acquired scans.
iii. Segmentation: The segregation of brain tissues like WM, GM and Cerebrospinal
fluid (CSF) is known as tissue segmentation. Segmentation is an essential phase
where the emphasis is on the individual tissue rather than the whole brain. In this
work, segmentation is performed as Parkinson’s majorly affects GM regions. Hence,
the features are extracted only from the GM.
iv. Smoothening: The co-registered MRI scans have undergone smoothening where a
pixel value is replaced by the weighted average of the neighbouring pixels.
v. Spatial Normalization: The co-registration of the subject’s MRI scan to the stand-
ard template is known as spatial normalization. To reduce the variability of the size
and shape of the head, spatial normalization is performed on each subject’s MRI
scan. Standard MNI template has been utilized for performing spatial normalization
on the International dataset i.e. the PPMI database. However, standard Indian template
has been utilized for performing normalization on the Indian dataset acquired from the
SWADESH database. The Indian template has been acquired from the online portal
of SWADESH database.
Figure 1 presents the screenshots of pre-processing techniques.
5  Feature extraction
This section describes the feature extraction techniques that have been employed in this
work. It includes wavelet transform and LBP along with its variants. These are explained
below:
5.1  Wavelet transform
Fourier Transform (FT) is capable of transforming an image of the spatial domain to its
frequency domain [21]. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) can effectively compute Dis-
crete Fourier Transform (DFT) that too with lower complexity. Short-Time Fourier Trans-
form (STFT) has the ability to analyse non-stationary signals, unlike FFT. However, for
signals with high frequency in a shorter time period, Wavelet transform is needed [29]. For

solution for most functions etc. [29]. Henceforth, DWT is commonly used.

5.2  Linear Binary Pattern (LBP) and its variants
A 2-dimensional LBP can be used for extracting pertinent features [33]. This technique
can effectively gauge structural as well as statistical information. It computes the LBP
value for an individual pixel by comparing its intensity with the neighbouring pixels.
Computed LBP values are capable of capturing the distribution of microstructures i.e.
edges. The LBP value can be calculated as presented in Eqs. (16) and (17).

However, this technique yields an extensive number of bins i.e. ­218 bins = 262,144
bins. Hence, it is necessary to reduce it further. Uniform and rotational invariant meth-
ods can be utilized to minimise bins/ narrow them down. Uniform LBP variants can
contain at most two ‘0 to 1’ or ‘1 to 0’ transformations [1, 32]. Hence, for an n-bit
binary number i.e. for n number of neighbours, the number of binary patterns will be as
presented in Eq. (20).
Uniform LBP = n × (n −1) + 3   (20)
The number of bins in the histogram for uniform LBP will be relatively less i.e. 309
(for 18 neighbouring voxels) as compared to 3D LBP i.e. 262,144. Subsequently, uni-
form LBP will now be mentioned as LBP-309.
Whereas the uniform rotation invariant LBP takes into account all the patterns
deduced by shifting the original pattern one bit to the right till the same arrangement
has been obtained [32]. This technique results in (n + 2) bins for n-bit binary numbers.
Since this work considers 18 neighbouring pixels, hence this technique results in 20 bins
or 20 features for describing individual slices. Hence, this method would be referred to
as LBP-20.
Comparative analysis of variations of LBP has been performed w.r.t. accuracy, sen-
sitivity and specificity. Table 5 presents the performance analysis of LBP variations on
the PPMI database and Indian dataset.
5.3  Combination of wavelet transform and LBP
The size of the feature set retrieved from the wavelet transform technique is huge thereby
enhancing the time complexity. Although LBP-20 extracts a relatively lower number of
features, however, it may lose sensitive information. Whereas LBP-309 has outperformed
other LBP variations w.r.t. accuracy, sensitivity and specificity. Therefore, a combination
of DWT and LBP-309 has been proposed in this work which reduces the time and space
complexity to a greater extent. Henceforth, it will be termed 3D-DWT + LBP-309.

The amalgamation of feature extraction techniques is capable of providing additional
data which an independent extraction technique fails to provide. Although, the combina-
tion results in enhanced performance of the decision model, it often leads to a relatively
enormous feature vector. Therefore, it is essential to utilize feature selection techniques for
eliminating irrelevant and redundant features [1].
6  Feature selection
It is essential to choose optimum features from the set of extracted features as all the fea-
tures may not take part in classification equivalently [21]. Hence, relevant features must be
selected based on their relevance. Fisher Discriminant Ratio (FDR) has been utilized for
selecting relevant features. FDR assigns scores to each feature depending on its capability
to participate in the classification process. Features with greater FDR scores are considered
crucial.
FDR score can be calculated by using Eq. (21).

7  ML Techniques and cross‑validation
There are a number of existing ML techniques that can be utilized for classification [3,
17].This section presents the ML-based classifiers that have been utilized for training
the model. It also describes the cross-validation technique employed in this work. The
performance evaluation measures are also presented in this section.
7.1  ML algorithms
In this work, four supervised learning algorithms namely: SVM, RF, LR and K-NN have
been employed to perform classification between Parkinson’s patients and healthy con-
trols. These are explained below:
a) SVM
SVM is a popular classifier which gives a better diagnostic performance in binary
classification. SVM iteratively creates a hyperplane and selects the one which classifies
the data points between the two classes with a maximum margin [9].
1 3
--- page 16 ---
46026   Multimedia Tools and Applications (2023) 82:46011–46036
b) Random forest (RF)
RF is a category of ensemble classification where multiple classifiers are employed
to enhance the classification performance [39]. It uses a combination of decision trees
which are trained on the subset of given data. Lastly, the output of the random forest
is determined via a majority vote of these decision trees. The complete process of the
random forest includes two phases namely: training and testing phase. In the training
phase, decision trees are constructed and trained on the dataset. While the testing phase
conducts the majority vote and the outcome is determined. More number of decision
trees results in maximum accuracy and it also prevents overfitting. It is identical to the
bagging technique as both employ a combination of decision trees produced from several
bootstrap samples via a majority vote. In this work, the number of trees was optimized
over (100, 200, 500, and 1000).
c) Logistic Regression (LR)
In LR, the binary dependent variable is modelled using a logistic function [28]. LR
has been widely used in the medical domain. It has the capability of describing data
accurately and has the potential to explain the relationship between one dependent vari-
able and one or more independent variables.
d) K-NN
K-NN is the most simple supervised learning algorithm. First, the model is trained
using training data [30]. K-NN then predicts the outcome of the test data by using a
similarity measure w.r.t. the trained data. K stands for the number of neighbours. Mostly,
Euclidean distance is employed to determine the distance between the samples. K is a
crucial parameter which must be selected consciously as it is important to strike a bal-
ance between underfitting and overfitting.
7.2  Cross‑validation
The traditional train split model divides/dissects the data randomly into training data and
testing data. Mostly, the training set consists of 80% data and testing is performed on the
rest 20%. It is generally used on larger datasets where training is required only once. How-
ever, the major limitation of traditional splitting is that the random splitting of data leads to
variations in performance accuracy. Also, it fails badly/poorly for datasets which are evenly
distributed as it may result in diversity in training and testing sets.
Shortcomings of the traditional train split model can be managed by K fold cv [42]. In
this, a k value is chosen as per the requirement which serves as the number of folds. The
dataset is then divided into k equal folds. The training set comprises (k-1) folds and the last
fold is used for the testing phase. Then the model is trained. This process is repeated till each
fold is used for testing exactly once. In this work, a tenfold cv has been utilized. In tenfold cv,
the dataset has been divided randomly into 10 equal subsets [4]. In each fold, 9 subsets are
utilized for training and one for testing. As the number of folds has been chosen as 10, the
experiment has been performed 10 times where each subset is used for testing exactly once.
7.3  Performance evaluation measures
The validation of the ML-based proposed system has been conducted via performance
evaluation measures i.e. Accuracy (ACC), Sensitivity (SENS) and Specificity (SPEC) [30].
These can be computed by using follows equations: Eqs. (22) to (24).

The pipeline of the proposed work has been depicted in Fig. 2.
Algorithm for Diagnosis of PD vs. HC
For the given data
1. Perform pre-processing to enhance the quality of the dataset.
2. Divide the data into training and testing sets.
3. For each MRI volume in the train set, perform the following:
a) Utilize 3D DWT for extracting 7 detailed components from each MRI.
b) Obtain features for each of the 7 components via 3D LBP and its variants.
c) Merge the obtained features from 3D- DWT and LBP-309 in a total of 2163 features
from 7 volumes.
4. For the selection of relevant features, apply FDR in decreasing order. This will be used
in testing.
5. Train the model using the training set.
6. Repeat the second step for the test data. Indices acquired in the third step are used for
representing MRI volumes. Evaluate the performance of the proposed model via per-
formance parameters accuracy, sensitivity and specificity.

9  Discussion
As per the experimental results presented in Table 7, the following can be concluded:
• Amongst 3D-DWT and the variants of LBP, 3D LBP gave the worst performance
while LBP-309 outperformed others.
• The proposed technique 3D-DWT + LBP 309 is efficient as it compactly represents
the MRI volume in terms of the distribution of different patterns from the detailed
components retrieved from 3D-DWT.
• The proposed technique 3D-DWT + LBP 309 has achieved an accuracy of 92.45%,
a sensitivity of 93.16% and a specificity of 91.74% for PPMI dataset. An accuracy
of 90.57%, sensitivity of 90.83% and specificity of 89.51% has been achieved by the
proposed technique when applied on the Indian dataset.
• The fusion of 3D- DWT and LBP 309 gives superior performance in comparison to
individual feature extraction techniques like 3D-DWT, 3D-LBP, LBP 309 and LBP-20
after a certain number of features.
To understand the superior performance of the proposed technique 3D DWT +
LBP 309 in comparison to the LBP-309 technique, the features of each technique are
normalized. Then, for each class, the average value of the individual feature has been com-
puted for both methods. These two methods have been compared w.r.t. their capability to
distinguish between the two classes.
Figure 8 presents the comparison between normalized features obtained via LBP 309
and 3D DWT + LBP 309 where DW1, DW2….DW7 refers to the seven detailed compo-
nents retrieved via 3D- DWT.
It can be concluded that the maximum difference in the values of LBP-309 is 0.3 while
that of 3D-DWT + LBP 309 is 0.68 thereby suggesting that the proposed technique is

10  Conclusion
PD is a degenerative disorder of the nervous system which is irreversible, incurable and
progresses gradually. Manual detection may lead to its misdiagnosis. Although research-
ers have proposed various techniques for Parkinson’s diagnosis. However, they are found
unsuitable to be used clinically due to their poor diagnostic performances. This work

proposes a novel PD detection technique based on sMRI scans retrieved from two sources
namely: the PPMI database and the Indian dataset. Interesting features have been extracted
via 3D-DWT, 3D-LBP, LBP-309 and LBP-20 from GM regions of the brain. The number
of features retrieved via 3D-DWT is humungous thereby making it complex to train the
1 3
--- page 24 ---
46034   Multimedia Tools and Applications (2023) 82:46011–46036
model. On the other hand, LBP-20 obtained the least number of features i.e. 20 however,
some fine details may be missed out. Also, among the various variants of LBP, LBP-309
outperformed. Therefore, this work has proposed a combination of 3D-DWT and LBP-309
for extracting pertinent features. The proposed combination solves the problem of miss-
ing details and larger feature sets thereby providing an optimal solution. This study has
employed four classifiers namely: SVM, RF, LR and K-NN where the former gave promis-
ing results. From the experiments, the tree size of 500 and K value of 7 have been found as
optimized for RF and K-NN respectively. The proposed technique performs better than the
state-of-art techniques that too with a relatively lesser number of features for the detection
of PD from normal individuals thereby paving the way for the clinical diagnosis.
In the future, multi-class classification will be performed for the proposed methods
and multivariate techniques can be utilized for feature selection. Also, more efficient
feature extraction techniques can be used in the future for improving the diagnostic
capability of the model.
